 Thanksgiving price hikes highlight the need for ‘more investment, not invention’ in agrifood
 November 18, 2026 | Jennifer Marston 
 Climate & sustainability 
 Investing 
 Research & data 
 Supply chain 
 Climate change has emerged as a structural driver of rising food prices, according to a new report from the Climate Action Campaign. 
 Image credit: iStock 
 Climate change has come for Thanksgiving pies according to a new report by the Climate Action Campaign that lays out the scale of crop loss and damage impacting some of the US holiday’s most classic food staples.
 Apples, pecans, and pumpkins as well as coffee and wheat are among the crops mentioned in the report.
 The impacts ripple up and down the food supply chain, from the farm gate into food processing and grocery. The average consumer planning a Thanksgiving dinner will see the impact most clearly in the cost of food, and that’s unlikely to change in coming years as climate change advances.
 “You may still have a pie on your table this Thanksgiving, but chances are, some of the ingredients will be less available and cost more because of our changing climate,” notes the report before bluntly stating that climate change is “putting your Thanksgiving favorites in jeopardy.”
 Price ‘rarely comes back down’ 
 “Climate change has emerged as a structural driver of rising food prices, and its influence is growing,” noted David Ortega, a professor of food economics and policy at Michigan State University.
 “As extreme heat, drought, and flooding disrupt more of the agri-food system, we can expect it to play a larger role in what consumers pay at the grocery store in the years ahead.”
 During a webinar this week discussing Climate Action’s new report, Ortega said climate change’s impact differs from other food system shocks felt over the last several years, such as the Covid-19 pandemic, tariffs, and the ongoing Middle East conflict.
 “Those are what I call acute shocks that impact the food system,” he said. “They’re very short-lived, and it’s very clear when you have that spike in the overall price level for food.”
 By contrast, impacts of climate change are slow but steady on prices, he added. See chocolate, prices for which have risen for years and quadrupled between 2023 and 2025 because of extreme weather in cacao-producing regions.
 “Once the price level increases, it very rarely comes down,” Ortega noted.
 “Crops like apples, cocoa, wheat, and corn need certain temperatures and precipitation levels to thrive, so a spring season that’s too wet or a summer that’s too warm and dry can damage crops and lead to farmers spending more resources on irrigation and other inputs, driving up prices,” explains the Climate Action report.
 In a growing number of cases, it also means crop loss. Apples, for example, had a rough year in the US thanks to a late spring frost that hit multiple states and forced growers to cancel fall picking seasons. The United States Department of Agriculture estimates a 7% decrease in 2026 apple yields compared to the previous year.
 In Texas, some growers say pumpkin crops were “nearly wiped out this year” by extreme heat, while further west, wildfire smoke impacted pollinator populations and “led to the worst pumpkin harvest in decades,” according to the report.
 Wheat also had a bad year—its worst in about 40, Dr. Omanjana Goswami, a food and environment scientist with the Union of Concerned Scientists, said during the webinar.
 She added that food-insecure families and individuals tend to bear the brunt of these hikes.
 More investment, not invention 
 While it’s not the lightest fare to digest around the holidays, panelists at the webinar agreed that more discussion of these matters is critical.
 “It’s something we’ve been dealing with for a number of years now,” Ortega said of the climate-related price hikes. “It’s having real impact, especially on the most vulnerable population, but the one bright spot of this, if there is one, is that it’s allowing us to have these conversations. It’s putting the spotlight on, well, what are these drivers that are leading to our food costing more, our inputs going up.”
 He added: “Especially when it comes to climate change, we have to restore the resources and the funding and the research and development in food and agriculture that makes our food system much more resilient to climate impacts.”
 Goswami said it was a matter of needing more investments in science, not more invention.
 “Solutions exist. We don’t need to go back to the lab and build from the ground up. It is now a matter of investing in the right science and the right programs, and putting this money into the hands of farmers who want to make this change.”
